catalog_quote: Phonologically, pidgin Tukang Besi differs from its parent in that the imploded stops /ɓ/ and /ɗ/ become /b/ and /d/, and the bilabial fricative that in standard Tukang Besi varies between [β], [ɸ] and [ʋ] becomes [w] in the pidgin. For some speakers V1ʔV1 and V1V1 sequences reduce to V1: (4) (individual words) a. ngaa ro'o mohii pe'esa- tee te'e name leaf left self tea water b. nga ro mohi pesa te te This affects the placement of the stress, which is usually penultimate. In both languages, high vowels tend to desyllabify in pre-stressed syllables, but this is more noticeable in the pidgin.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing stress statement for pidg1257, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict; this is the first primary statement found for the pidgin and it should enter the catalog as a new record (penultimate, hedged 'usually', source Donohue 1996:714). It is consistent with the previously checked Donohue 1995 thesis on the parent language Tukang Besi (tuka1249), whose section 2.3.2 gives penultimate stress; Donohue 1996 explicitly says 'in both languages'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in pidgin Tukang Besi falls on the penultimate syllable ('usually penultimate'), as in the parent language Tukang Besi. Because some speakers contract V1ʔV1 and identical-vowel sequences to a single vowel (ngaa > nga, ro'o > ro, pe'esa > pesa), the syllable count changes and the penultimate stress lands on a different vowel than in the full language; high vowels in pre-stressed syllables tend to desyllabify (glide), more so in the pidgin, which likewise shifts the syllable that counts as penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. The only other prosodic remark is on example (5), where the author marks pitch/intonation levels over 'Te iaku pe'esa-su' vs 'Yaku pesa' and says 'There are three intonational levels in 5a, but only two in 5b' — a phrase-intonation observation, not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'usually'; no explicit exceptions listed. Vowel-sequence reduction (V1ʔV1, V1V1 > V1, 'for some speakers') and desyllabification of high vowels in pre-stressed syllables alter where the penult falls, so surface stress position varies by speaker between contracted and uncontracted forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Donohue 1996 describes 'pidgin Tukang Besi', the trade-language variety used by Tukang Besi islanders in their settlements across eastern Indonesia (Maluku, Nusa Tenggara, coastal Irian Jaya, southern Sulawesi, Borneo, Sumatra, Java, Singapore), and states the stress rule as holding 'in both languages' (the pidgin and standard Tukang Besi). The same chapter separately mentions a 'Tukang Besi pre-pidgin at Fakfak, Irian Jaya' (a few trade words only; no phonological statement). The atlas citation string in the target record names the Ehrhart-Kneher & Corne Tayo chapter (pp. 265–270); that chapter is about New Caledonia and is irrelevant to this language — the chapter that Glottolog reference 57587 actually attaches to pidg1257 is Donohue's, vol. 2:2 pp. 713–716.
